claim: Categorization of everyday objects requires that humans form representations of shape that are tolerant to variations among exemplars.
source: Categorization of everyday objects requires that humans form representations of shape that are tolerant to variations among exemplars.
evidence: This is a general statement about object categorization that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: How invariant shape representations develop remains poorly understood.
source: Yet, how such invariant shape representations develop remains poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and identifies a gap in understanding.

claim: Human infants (6–12 months; N=82) classified novel objects across variations in their component parts following habituation to a never-before-seen object.
source: Following habituation to a never-before-seen object, infants classified other novel objects across variations in their component parts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Infants' performance was best described by a model of shape based on the skeletal structure.
source: Comparisons to several computational models of vision, including models of high-level and low-level vision, revealed that infants' performance was best described by a model of shape based on the skeletal structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing infant performance to computational models.

claim: Infants outperformed a range of artificial neural network models under the same conditions.
source: Interestingly, infants outperformed a range of artificial neural network models, selected for their massive object experience and biological plausibility, under the same conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparative analysis between infants and ANNs.

claim: Robust representations of shape can be formed with little language or object experience by relying on the perceptually invariant skeletal structure.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that robust representations of shape can be formed with little language or object experience by relying on the perceptually invariant skeletal structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about infant performance.

claim: Shape information is crucial for object categorization.
source: Although there is widespread agreement that shape information is crucial for object categorization (Biederman, 1995; Mervis and Rosch, 1981), it remains unclear how humans come to form global representations of shape that are tolerant to variations among exemplars.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Linguistic experience, particularly the learning of object labels, draws children's attention to global shape as a diagnostic cue, inducing a 'shape bias'.
source: It has been suggested that global shape information becomes crucial for object categorization in early childhood because linguistic experience, particularly the learning of object labels (e.g. 'dog'), draws children's attention to global shape as a diagnostic cue—inducing a so-called 'shape bias' (Landau et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1996; Smith et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Labels may bootstrap object recognition abilities in prelinguistic children.
source: Indeed, labels may bootstrap object recognition abilities more generally, such that even prelinguistic children are better at individuating and categorizing objects when verbal labels are provided (Ferry et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Supervised artificial neural networks have begun to match the object recognition abilities and neural representations of human adults.
source: Indeed, several studies suggest that motion information may initially bootstrap infants' ability to extract 3D shape structure (Kellman and Arterberry, 2006; Ostrovsky et al., 2009; Wood and Wood, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ANNs may develop a shape bias that supports object categorization when generalizing across variations in color or texture with appropriate experience.
source: With appropriate experience, these models may even develop a shape bias that supports object categorization, at least when generalizing across variations in color or texture (Ritter et al., 2017; Tartaglini et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The shape skeleton is a quantitative model that describes an object's global shape via a series of internal symmetry axes.
source: One such property is known as the shape skeleton—a quantitative model that describes an object's global shape via a series of internal symmetry axes (Blum, 1967; Feldman and Singh, 2006).
evidence: This claim defines the shape skeleton and is supported by citations.

claim: Models of skeletal structure are tolerant to local variations in shape typical of basic-level exemplars.
source: These axes define the topological arrangement of object parts, making models of skeletal structure tolerant to local variations in shape typical of basic-level exemplars (Ayzenberg et al., 2019a; Wilder et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Newborns can discriminate between simple 2D shapes.
source: Using this approach, researchers have shown that newborns can already discriminate between simple 2D shapes (Slater et al., 1983) and display shape constancy, such that they recognize a shape from a novel orientation (Slater and Morison, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: By 6 months of age, infants can categorize objects using only the stimulus' shape silhouette.
source: By 6 months of age, infants' shape representations are also robust to variations among category exemplars, such that they can categorize objects using only the stimulus' shape silhouette (Quinn et al., 1993; Quinn et al., 2001a), as well as extend category membership to objects with varying local contours, but the same global shape (Quinn et al., 2002; Quinn et al., 2001b; Turati et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual experience at 6-12 months of age is dominated by just a few common objects (~10 objects).
source: We chose to test 6–12-month-olds because the visual experience at this age is dominated by just a few common objects (~10 objects; Clerkin et al., 2017) and they have relatively little linguistic understanding (~7 words; Bergelson and Swingley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 6-12 month old infants have relatively little linguistic understanding (~7 words).
source: We chose to test 6–12-month-olds because the visual experience at this age is dominated by just a few common objects (~10 objects; Clerkin et al., 2017) and they have relatively little linguistic understanding (~7 words; Bergelson and Swingley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 1, infants looked longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[33]=3.04, p=0.005, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.16, 0.88], BF10=8.42).
source: A comparison of the two types of test trials in Experiment 1 (Figure 2A) revealed that, across the test phase, infants looked longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[33]=3.04, p=0.005, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.16, 0.88], BF10=8.42; Figure 2B), with the majority of infants showing this effect (25/34 infants, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: The majority of infants in Experiment 1 showed longer looking times at objects with different skeletons (25/34 infants, p=0.009).
source: A comparison of the two types of test trials in Experiment 1 (Figure 2A) revealed that, across the test phase, infants looked longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[33]=3.04, p=0.005, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.16, 0.88], BF10=8.42; Figure 2B), with the majority of infants showing this effect (25/34 infants, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, dishabituation only occurred for the object with the different skeleton (t[33]=3.36, p=0.002, d=0.58, 95% CI [0.21, 0.94], BF10=17.47).
source: In addition, a comparison between the end of habituation (mean of last 4 trials) and looking times across the test phase revealed that dishabituation only occurred for the object with the different skeleton (t[33]=3.36, p=0.002, d=0.58, 95% CI [0.21, 0.94], BF10=17.47; 25/34 infants, p=0.009), not the object with the matching skeleton (t[33]=1.00, p=0.325, d=0.17, 95% CI [–0.16, 0.51], BF10=0.29; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 1, dishabituation did not occur for the object with the matching skeleton (t[33]=1.00, p=0.325, d=0.17, 95% CI [–0.16, 0.51], BF10=0.29).
source: In addition, a comparison between the end of habituation (mean of last 4 trials) and looking times across the test phase revealed that dishabituation only occurred for the object with the different skeleton (t[33]=3.36, p=0.002, d=0.58, 95% CI [0.21, 0.94], BF10=17.47; 25/34 infants, p=0.009), not the object with the matching skeleton (t[33]=1.00, p=0.325, d=0.17, 95% CI [–0.16, 0.51], BF10=0.29; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: Infants treated objects with matching skeletons as more similar to one another than objects with different skeletons.
source: Thus, infants treated objects with matching skeletons as more similar to one another than objects with different skeletons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on looking times.

claim: Infants were capable of discriminating objects on the basis of surface form alone.
source: This analysis revealed that infants were indeed capable of discriminating objects on the basis of surface form alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of first test trial looking times.

claim: Infants dishabituated to the object with the same skeleton but different surface form (t(15) = 3.76, p=0.002, d=0.94, 95% CI [0.34, 1.52], BF10=22.23).
source: That is, infants dishabituated to the object with the same skeleton but different surface form, t(15) = 3.76, p=0.002, d=0.94, 95% CI [0.34, 1.52], BF10=22.23, with the majority of infants showing this effect (14/16, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: Infants' looking times on the first test trial did not differ for either test object (8.31 s vs. 9.18 s; t[32]=0.50, p=0.624, d=.17, 95% CI [–0.51, 0.84], BF10=0.36).
source: Moreover, and crucially, infants' looking times on the first test trial did not differ for either test object (8.31 s vs. 9.18 s; t[32]=0.50, p=0.624, d=.17, 95% CI [–0.51, 0.84], BF10=0.36).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: The two types of test objects were matched for discriminability relative to the habituation object.
source: These findings demonstrate that not only could infants differentiate between surface forms, but also, that the two types of test objects were matched for discriminability relative to the habituation object.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on looking times.

claim: All computational models tested performed above chance in Experiment 1.
source: These analyses revealed that all models performed above chance (0.50; see Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Infant performance was best matched to the Skeletal model in Experiment 1.
source: However, and importantly, infant performance was best matched to the Skeletal model.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant performance to computational models.

claim: Both infants and the Skeletal model performed significantly better than all other models except FlowNet in Experiment 1.
source: Both infants and the Skeletal model performed significantly better than all other models, except FlowNet.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of model performance.

claim: FlowNet's performance did not differ from that of any ANN or the Pixel model in Experiment 1.
source: However, the success of FlowNet does suggest that motion information may contribute to representations of shape. Nevertheless, FlowNet's performance did not differ from that of any ANN or the Pixel model, leaving its exact role in object classification unclear.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of model performance.

claim: In Experiment 2, infants looked longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[47]=2.60, p=0.012, d=0.38, 95% CI [0.08, 0.67], BF10=3.18).
source: However, we found that infants continued to look longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[47]=2.60, p=0.012, d=0.38, 95% CI [0.08, 0.67], BF10=3.18; Figure 2E), with the majority of infants showing this effect (33/48 infants, p=0.013).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: The majority of infants in Experiment 2 showed longer looking times at objects with different skeletons (33/48 infants, p=0.013).
source: However, we found that infants continued to look longer at the object with the different skeleton compared to the one with the matching skeleton (t[47]=2.60, p=0.012, d=0.38, 95% CI [0.08, 0.67], BF10=3.18; Figure 2E), with the majority of infants showing this effect (33/48 infants, p=0.013).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, infants only dishabituated during the test phase to the object with the different skeleton (t[47]=3.63, p<0.001, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.22, 0.82], BF10=39.77; 36/48 infants, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, infants only dishabituated during the test phase to the object with the different skeleton (t[47]=3.63, p<0.001, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.22, 0.82], BF10=39.77; 36/48 infants, p<0.001), not the one with the matching skeleton (t[47]=1.42, p=0.163, d=0.16, 95% CI [–0.08, 0.49], BF10=0.40), as in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, infants did not dishabituate to the object with the matching skeleton (t[47]=1.42, p=0.163, d=0.16, 95% CI [–0.08, 0.49], BF10=0.40).
source: Moreover, infants only dishabituated during the test phase to the object with the different skeleton (t[47]=3.63, p<0.001, d=0.52, 95% CI [0.22, 0.82], BF10=39.77; 36/48 infants, p<0.001), not the one with the matching skeleton (t[47]=1.42, p=0.163, d=0.16, 95% CI [–0.08, 0.49], BF10=0.40), as in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: The results from Experiment 2 rule out the possibility that infants classified objects on the basis of their coarse spatial relations, rather than their shape skeletons.
source: The results from this experiment rule out the possibility that infants classified objects on the basis of their coarse spatial relations, rather than their shape skeletons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings of Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, infants dishabituated to the object with the same shape skeleton but different surface form (t(22)=3.51, p=0.002, d=0.73, 95% CI [0.26, 1.19], BF10=19.71).
source: We found that infants dishabituated to the object with the same shape skeleton but different surface form, t(22)=3.51, p=0.002, d=0.73, 95% CI [0.26, 1.19], BF10=19.71, with the majority of infants showing this effect (17/23, p=0.035), suggesting that discrimination was possible on the basis of surface form alone.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, infants' looking times on the first test trial did not differ for the two types of test objects (6.87 s vs. 10.83 s; t[45]=1.47, p=0.149, d=0.43, 95% CI [–0.15, 1.00], BF10=0.69).
source: Moreover, infants' looking times on the first test trial did not differ for the two types of test objects (6.87 s vs. 10.83 s; t[45]=1.47, p=0.149, d=0.43, 95% CI [–0.15, 1.00], BF10=0.69), confirming comparable discriminability.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical support.

claim: In Experiment 2, the Skeletal, Pixel, and FlowNet models all performed above chance.
source: These analyses revealed that the Skeletal, Pixel, and FlowNet models all performed above chance (Figure 2F), but infant performance was most closely matched to the Skeletal model.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: In Experiment 2, none of the ANNs performed above chance.
source: None of the ANNs performed above chance.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, infant performance was most closely matched to the Skeletal model.
source: These analyses revealed that the Skeletal, Pixel, and FlowNet models all performed above chance (Figure 2F), but infant performance was most closely matched to the Skeletal model.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant performance to computational models.

claim: In Experiment 2, both infants and the Skeletal model significantly outperformed the ANNs and the Pixel model, but not FlowNet.
source: As in Experiment 1, both infants and the Skeletal model significantly outperformed the ANNs and the Pixel model, but not FlowNet.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of model performance.

claim: ResNet-IN, CorNet-S, and ResNext-SAY performed above chance (Ms = 0.62–0.66, 95% CIs [0.53–0.59, 0.70–0.76]) when classifying objects by surface form using stimuli from Experiment 1.
source: Using a comparable procedure to the previous experiments, all models were tested with objects in which the surface forms either matched or differed from the habituated object; both test objects differed in their shape skeletons (Figure 3A). For objects from Experiment 1 (Figure 1), the analyses revealed that ResNet-IN, CorNet-S, and ResNext-SAY performed above chance (Ms = 0.62–0.66, 95% CIs [0.53–0.59, 0.70–0.76]; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis on surface form classification.

claim: Skeletal, ResNet-SIN, Pixel, and FlowNet models did not perform differently from chance (Ms = 0.52–0.61, 95% CIs [0.40–0.48, 0.60–0.72]) when classifying objects by surface form using stimuli from Experiment 1.
source: By contrast, none of the other models (Skeleton, ResNet-SIN, Pixel, FlowNet) performed differently from chance (Ms = 0.52–0.61, 95% CIs [0.40–0.48, 0.60–0.72]; Figure 3B) when classifying objects by surface form (i.e. across shape skeletons).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis on surface form classification.

claim: All models except Skeletal and Pixel models performed above chance (Ms = 0.67–0.74, 95% CIs [0.51–0.67, 0.72–0.80]) when classifying objects by surface form using stimuli from Experiment 2.
source: For objects from Experiment 2 (Figure 1), all models performed above chance (Ms = 0.67–0.74, 95% CIs [0.51–0.67, 0.72–0.80]), except Skeletal and Pixel models (Ms = 0.54–0.59, 95% CIs [0.40–0.41, 0.68–0.73]; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis on surface form classification.

claim: Most ANNs are capable of classifying objects using local shape properties.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that most ANNs are capable of classifying objects using local shape properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational model analysis on surface form classification.

claim: ANNs show sensitivity to local shape properties.
source: These findings are consistent with other research showing sensitivity to local shape properties in ANNs (Baker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Infants represent global shape by extracting a skeletal structure.
source: Here, we demonstrate that infants represent global shape by extracting a skeletal structure.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: With only one exemplar as a reference, infants classified objects by their shape skeletons across variations in local properties.
source: With only one exemplar as a reference, infants classified objects by their shape skeletons across variations in local properties that altered component parts of the objects, including when coarse spatial relations could not be used as a diagnostic cue.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary experimental findings.

claim: A Skeletal model provided the closest match to infants' performance.
source: Moreover, a Skeletal model provided the closest match to infants' performance, further suggesting that infants relied on the shape skeleton to determine object similarity.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing infant performance to computational models.

claim: The formation of robust shape representations in humans is largely rooted in sensitivity to the shape skeleton.
source: Based on these findings, we would argue that the formation of robust shape representations in humans is largely rooted in sensitivity to the shape skeleton, an invariant representation of global shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: When generalizing across the surface form, a Pixel model performed above chance.
source: In particular, when generalizing across the surface form, a Pixel model performed above chance.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: Both infants and the Skeletal model outperformed the Pixel model in both experiments.
source: Second, both infants and the Skeletal model outperformed the Pixel model in both experiments, further arguing against an account based on image-level similarity alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of model performance.

claim: Low-level visual similarity explains more variance in infants' behavioral and neural responses than the upper layers of ANNs.
source: Indeed, recent studies comparing the visual representations of infants and computational models reveal that low-level visual similarity explains more variance in infants' behavioral and neural responses than the upper layers of ANNs (Kiat et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Object categorization in infancy may be supported by the representations of the early visual cortex (V1-V3), rather than the higher-level ventral cortex, as in adults.
source: Moreover, recent studies suggest that object categorization in infancy may be supported by the representations of the early visual cortex (V1-V3), rather than the higher-level ventral cortex, as in adults (Spriet et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Skeletal representations may emerge in area V3 as a consequence of between-layer recurrent interactions among border-ownership cells in area V2 and grouping cells in area V3.
source: Specifically, several studies have suggested that skeletal representations may emerge in area V3 as a consequence of between-layer recurrent interactions among border-ownership cells in area V2 and grouping cells in area V3 (Ardila et al., 2012; Craft et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Representations of skeletal structures in V3 are invariant across changes in component parts.
source: Interestingly, representations of skeletal structures in V3 are invariant across changes in component parts, which lends support to their role in categorization (Ayzenberg et al., 2022; Lescroart and Biederman, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: V3 in primates shows evidence of functional maturity shortly after birth.
source: Other research on the anatomical and functional organization of V3 in primates shows evidence of functional maturity shortly after birth (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017; Ellis et al., 2020; Wiesel and Hubel, 1974), further raising the possibility that skeletal structure is represented in this area with little object experience or any language.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FlowNet appeared comparable to infants and the Skeletal model at classifying objects when they differed in surface form.
source: In the present study, we also found that FlowNet, a model of optic flow, appeared comparable to infants and the Skeletal model at classifying objects when they differed in surface form.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: Infants are better at recognizing objects from novel viewpoints when they are first familiarized with moving objects rather than static images.
source: It is known that infants are better at recognizing objects from novel viewpoints when they are first familiarized with moving objects rather than static images (Kellman, 1984; Kellman and Shipley, 1991; Kellman and Short, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Viewpoint-invariant object recognition in chicks occurs only if the chicks are raised in environments in which objects exhibit smooth, continuous motion.
source: Moreover, controlled-rearing studies with chicks have found that viewpoint-invariant object recognition occurs only if the chicks are raised in environments in which objects exhibit smooth, continuous motion (Wood and Wood, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Motion information may initially bootstrap infants' ability to extract 3D shape structure.
source: Indeed, several studies suggest that motion information may initially bootstrap infants' ability to extract 3D shape structure (Kellman and Arterberry, 2006; Ostrovsky et al., 2009; Wood and Wood, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Skeletal model was more closely aligned to the performance of human infants than was FlowNet.
source: Indeed, the Skeletal model, which does not incorporate any motion information, was more closely aligned to the performance of human infants than was FlowNet.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis of model performance.

claim: ANNs were not capable of classifying objects across variations in surface form.
source: In contrast to infants and the other models, ANNs were not capable of classifying objects across variations in surface form.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: ANNs were capable of classifying objects by their surface form (across variation in shape skeleton).
source: However, they were capable of classifying objects by their surface form (across variation in shape skeleton), ruling out alternative explanations for their poor performance in the first task based on idiosyncrasies of the stimuli or testing procedures.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: Conventional ANNs rely on qualitatively different mechanisms than do humans to represent objects.
source: Moreover, this finding suggests that, regardless of the specific architecture or training type, conventional ANNs rely on qualitatively different mechanisms than do humans to represent objects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational model analysis.

claim: ANNs may be especially sensitive to local object properties, making them susceptible to spurious changes in the objects' contours.
source: This class of models may be especially sensitive to local object properties, making them susceptible to spurious changes in the objects' contours (Baker et al., 2018; Baker et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Representations of skeletal structure in humans are particularly robust to perturbations.
source: By contrast, representations of skeletal structure in humans are particularly robust to perturbations (Ayzenberg et al., 2019a; Feldman and Singh, 2006) and, thus, may be especially well-suited to basic-level categorization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Conventional ANNs can generalize across variations in color and texture.
source: Although conventional ANNs (e.g. ResNet-SIN) can generalize across variations in color and texture (Geirhos et al., 2018; Tartaglini et al., 2022), fundamental changes to ANNs' architectures and/or training may be needed before they can achieve human-like categorization on the basis of global shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: By adulthood, humans also use visual properties such as texture and local contours, as well as inferential processes such as abstract rules and the object's generative history to reason about objects.
source: Indeed, by adulthood, humans also use visual properties such as texture (Jagadeesh and Gardner, 2022; Long et al., 2018) and local contours (Davitt et al., 2014), as well as inferential processes such as abstract rules (Ons and Wagemans, 2012; Rouder and Ratcliff, 2016) and the object's generative history (Fleming and Schmidt, 2019; Spröte et al., 2016) to reason about objects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Properties such as texture and local features may override shape skeletons in certain contexts, such as when identifying objects in the periphery or during subordinate-level categorization.
source: Properties such as texture and local features may even override shape skeletons in certain contexts, such as when identifying objects in the periphery (Gant et al., 2021) or during subordinate-level categorization (Davitt et al., 2014; Tarr and Bülthoff, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The shape skeleton may be uniquely suited to the basic level of categorization, wherein objects have similar global shapes but vary in their component parts.
source: We suggest that the shape skeleton may be uniquely suited to the basic level of categorization, wherein objects have similar global shapes but vary in their component parts (Biederman, 1995; Rosch et al., 1976).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Infants were habituated to a single, novel object to better understand the pre-existing visual representations infants rely on for object perception.
source: A key aspect of our design was that infants were habituated to a single, novel object. We did this to better understand the pre-existing visual representations infants rely on for object perception, rather than the ones they may learn over the course of habituation.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach and its rationale.

claim: Infants reliably classified objects on the basis of the shape skeleton using a single exemplar.
source: Using this approach, we found that infants reliably classified objects on the basis of the shape skeleton.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary experimental findings.

claim: One-shot categorization of objects by older children and adults involves identifying invariant visual properties of the objects, namely shape.
source: On the one hand, our results are consistent with studies showing that one-shot categorization of objects by older children and adults involves identifying invariant visual properties of the objects, namely shape (Biederman and Bar, 1999; Feldman, 1997; Landau et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A skeleton-like compositional structure is central to one-shot categorization using simple visual objects.
source: Moreover, research using simple visual objects (e.g. handwritten characters) suggests that a skeleton-like compositional structure is central to one-shot categorization (Lake et al., 2011; Lake et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One-shot category learning may be possible early in development by relying on a perceptually invariant skeletal structure.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with the hypothesis that one-shot category learning may be possible early in development by relying on a perceptually invariant skeletal structure.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: Experience with moving objects may play a role in supporting the extraction of a 3D shape structure.
source: As mentioned previously, experience with moving objects may play a role in supporting the extraction of a 3D shape structure.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on prior discussion and research.

claim: Infants' visual experience includes a large volume of viewpoints for each object.
source: Moreover, although infants' visual experience is dominated by a small number of objects, this experience includes a large volume of viewpoints for each object (Clerkin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Infants' chosen views of objects are biased toward planar orientations.
source: Interestingly, infants' chosen views of objects are biased toward planar orientations (James et al., 2014; Slone et al., 2019), which may serve to highlight the shape skeleton, though it is unclear whether such a bias is a consequence or a cause of skeletal extraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Certain visual experiences, such as low visual acuity at birth, may be particularly important for highlighting global shape information.
source: Moreover, certain visual experiences, such as low visual acuity at birth, may be particularly important for highlighting global shape information (Cassia et al., 2002; Ostrovsky et al., 2009).

claim: ANNs trained with a blurry-to-clear visual regimen showed improved performance for categories where global information is important, such as faces.
